headline: Gastwirth cautious on Space addition to Nasdaq 100, citing rich valuation set by Musk and unproven execution on long-term growth thesis
reasoning: Gastwirth observes that the stock showed no meaningful pop upon being added to the Nasdaq 100, which he views as a bearish signal given typical index-inclusion dynamics. He argues the IPO valuation was a take-it-or-leave-it set by Musk at a ~$1.95 trillion market cap and came at no discount. While acknowledging long-term optionality in Starlink and other segments, he sees current valuation as premature and execution risk as material.
quote: The interesting thing is the stock didn't basically nothing after this announcement. I mean we're still teeter tottering around that level of where it went to IPO at that one nine 5 or 1, you know, trillion dollar market cap. Um, you know, to me, this is a little bit of a bearish sign. I think typically when you have these companies added to indexes, you see a nice initial pop. Uh, and we did not at all. And I would also argue, I think it's a little premature to be added right now. I mean, the the company obviously was historic IPO, the largest ever. That being said, it did not come cheap and it was a take it or leave it which mean Musk created the valuation. And he said this is where it is. You take it or you leave it. Now, on a long term, you can make arguments that, yes, they can Starlink and grow into this mega communications, you know, business. And then the, you know, all these other aspects can be monstrous. But these are big ifs and you need the execution. To me, I'm not jumping in both right now at these levels.
episode_title: Hype for scale in the tech space

headline: Brad Gastwirth cautious on SpaceX IPO, questioning whether retail participation reflects genuine oversubscription or insufficient institutional demand

headline: Brad Gastwirth cautious on US-Iran peace deal being finalised, sees it as 50/50 at best despite market rally

He views the deal as 50/50 at best, pointing to repeated false starts over the past several weeks where a deal was said to be imminent but nothing was signed. He warns that a single act of terrorism by a group opposed to the deal could reignite conflict. Despite this near-term uncertainty, he remains broadly bullish on markets over the next 24 months.
quote: Yeah. I mean look the markets Andrew, over the last you know, 36 months have really ignored macro related events. If you look at even, you know, further back, five years ago with the initial US-China tech issues and the different tariffs then moving on to Russia, Ukraine, then looking at Israel and Gaza, then looking at, you know, this Iran conflict. There's been time and time again that these markets have completely ignored the macro, you know, events. And I still think that there's a lot of uncertainty here coming from the Middle East. You know, will it be a complete done deal? All it takes is one of these terrorist groups that does not want the deal to do a bombing. And then all of a sudden you'll see fighting for both sides. So I don't think this is, you know, a done deal. Is it a little premature? Possibly. I mean, I'm still quite bullish on the markets. I still think you're going to see significant increases over the next 24 months. That being said, I don't think the conflict over here is over it just yet.
